rv.q: When the servants are just as winning as the leads, that tells you this is one regal and enjoyable “Royal Family.”
There's a beauty of one now in "The Royal Family," the classic 1927 comedy that George S. Kaufman and Edna Ferber wrote about three generations of a chaotic and madly gifted New York acting dynasty.
Both women are wonderful paradoxes, people for whom artifice is truly natural, and as mother and daughter they communicate in a perfect private language to which we are allowed privileged access.

This handsome Broadway revival of Edna Ferber and George S. Kaufman's 1927 backstage comedy about a theatrical dynasty gets by on old-fashioned star power and polished craft, even if the material shows its age.
Thanks to Maxwell and Rogers, for the moment their bygone spirit is burning brightly once again.

Scenery-munching is allowed, and the cast's incisors are sharp, for the most part. Director Doug Hughes keeps the plots spinning smoothly. Reigning over the three-ring circus is grande dame Fanny (a restrained Rosemary Harris), who's been out of commission for two years but is ready for a comeback.
In the end, the actors pull it off, proving that when fine players such as these, in the tradition of the Barrymores, take to the stage, they are a delight to behold.

cn.t: This 1927 Kaufman-Ferber comedy about a theatrical dynasty gets a rousing, sumptuous revival with standout performances from Jan Maxwell and Reg Rogers, though ensemble work could be tighter and laughs don't always reach gale-force.

vs.sum: The Samuel J. Friedman Theatre offers good sightlines with minimal obstructions and a well-raked mezzanine, ensuring a clear view from most seats. The sound quality is consistently praised, and the seating is comfortable with decent legroom. The theater's ambiance is enhanced by its elegant design following renovation, though facilities like restrooms are average, leading to some congestion during intermissions.

acc.note: Elevator to all levels. Built-in induction loop for t-coil hearing aids.
